Not long ago, a sudden glacier collapse in the China-Nepal border area has triggered a severe mudslide. causing significant casualties and leaving people missing on both sides. China extends its condolences to the government of Nepal and all those hit by this disaster, and sincerely hopes that they will restore their livelihoods and rebuild their homes at an early date. China and Nepal are a community linked by mountains and rivers, and sharing a common future. As both countries have suffered from this cross-border disaster, we deeply understand each other's pain and share a common aspiration to strengthen the protection of mountains and glaciers and enhance early warning and disaster relief capabilities. While carrying out rescue and relief efforts at home, China extended a helping hand to Nepal at an early stage moment. by dispatching rescue experts, sharing important information such as images, satellite and hydrological data of the disaster-driven area. China supported Nepal in its emergency disaster relief efforts. In the face of disaster, our two countries have interpreted the tradition of friendship across the Himalayas with concrete actions. Colleagues, climate change is a common challenge for humankind, we must fully implement the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and its Paris Agreement, remain remitting in actions and relentless in intensity, and firmly pursue a path of green and low carbon development. Faced with climate risks, developing countries have an urgent need to strengthen their adoption capabilities. while also shouldering the important task of energy transition and economic development. At the same time, they should advance energy transition in light of their national circumstances and the resources endowment. China is an active promoter and contributor to global climate governance. Climate change and green development is one of the eight priority areas of the Global Development Initiative proposed by President Xi Jinping. We stand ready to work with all parties to address climate change, advance a just and green transition, and build a clean and beautiful world together. Thank you, Ambassador.
Thank you so much. Now I would like to invite Ms. Thelmidja Hussein, Director, Regional Commissions, Office of New York, as a co-host of this event.

Honorable Foreign Minister of Nepal, Shis Kunal, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, it is a pleasure to join you today and particularly to see this important conversation continue from Bangkok to New York. I would also like to recognize his Excellency, Lok Bahadur Thapa, under whose presidency of ECOSOC we had this discussion earlier at ESCAP during APFST. Sagar Matar to the sea, strengthening the foundation for this conversation we are carrying forward here today. Allow me to also express, join others in expressing our condolences to the end. From mountains to small island states, this conversation captures precisely why this initiative matters. And we heard the impacts from loss of glaciers that are felt beyond the mountains, from rivers that sustain the communities to deltas where millions live, and coastlines where small island states homes their livelihoods and the increasingly at risk of losing their homes. Today, the opportunities to take conversation a little bit further from recognizing the connection to building cooperation around it. Across the five regions, the regional commissions have experience that can support and advance the action. as executive secretary also highlight, we can connect the climate data and early warning systems across borders. We can work together to manage shared rivers and risks that stretch from mountains to coastlines. And we can share practical approaches to adaptation and climate finance, particularly for vulnerable countries and mountainous countries and small island states across different regions. And this is where regional cooperation can make a real difference. Countries may face different challenges, but they're also finding solutions. And there's a lot we can learn from one another. The regional commissions are already working across Africa, Latin America, Caribbean, Asia Pacific, Western Asia on climate finance, including debt for climate swaps. And we can build on these approaches. What works in one region on early warning systems, water management, adaptation or finance can help shape solutions in others. And this was an important part of our conversation in Bangkok, and we should continue to build on this. So the regional commissions and along with the regional commissions, New York office, we stand ready to carry this dialogue across regions, sharing experiences, strengthening cooperation, advancing resilience from Sagar Mata to the shores of the Maldives and other small island states. Thank you. Now I would like to invite His Excellency, Mr. Ralph Regin Vanu, Minister of Climate Change of Vanuatu. Excellency, you have the floor.

Excellencies, colleagues, we thank the co-hosts for organizing this important event and share our condolences with the government and people of Nepal. We have heard how glacier loss and rising seas connect mountain and island communities. They also expose a shared injustice. Those least responsible face profound losses while having the least power over the response. Our communities are expected to demonstrate resilience, while borrowing to rebuild. Access to support too often depends on donor priorities, funding cycles, and what others are prepared to offer. Loss of life, damage to health and ecosystems, and losses of culture and relationships that sustain community life remain inadequately recognized. Climate justice requires us to confront who bears these costs and who controls the response. People should not have to depend on handouts from those most responsible for the harm on terms that those countries determine. The science, early warning, technology, and accessible finance discussed today are essential, but justice requires processes through which affected people can exercise their rights, determine their priorities, and secure remedy. The ICJ advisory opinion gave us legal clarity on this. Addressing the injury and loss and damage that is undermining our peoples and way of life is a matter of rights and obligations under international law. Our institutions must give all obligations relating to climate change practical effect and drive meaningful change. We know that if we continue on the present course, knowing the consequences, we are complicit in the harm. The General Assembly resolution we secured together in May this year, resolution 80/263, provides a process to advance the work. The final two paragraphs of the resolution are of critical importance. One requests the Secretary-General to report back to the General Assembly on ways to advance compliance with all obligations in relation to the court's findings. We spent months negotiating this paragraph. Vanuatu's original proposal was to establish an international register of climate damage and a mechanism for reparation of climate harms. The compromise was a stepped approach, a commitment to a process that could lead to establishing the register mechanism through the Secretary-General's report, provided there was no actual reference to it in the resolution itself. The silver lining to this compromise is that the concept of the register and the mechanism was socialized, and we have not abandoned these proposals. We want the report to help move them forward. An international register of climate damage and mechanism for reparation of climate harms would document economic and non-economic losses, including slow onset harm that receives too little attention. The mechanism would turn that evidence into remedy through cooperation, negotiated reparation, coordination of resources, and scrutiny of delivery. Working alongside existing funds and technical networks, these arrangements would help ensure that documented harm and affected communities' priorities guide the response. They would provide a standing process for pursuing repair, rather than leaving countries to renew appeals after each disaster. The Secretary-General's report is due after the UN's 82nd session. This session, UN 81, is the time to organize, build support, and contribute. It is a time to start building ideas on ways to advance compliance with obligations and operationalize the court's findings, and most importantly, coordinate on this. The second critical paragraph of resolution 80/263 is the follow-up of the advisory opinion being included on the agenda for UN 83. This is an opportunity that should not be overlooked because it is so far away. We should work on a General Assembly resolution that actions these proposed structural changes, the register and the mechanism for reparation. Unlike the incremental gains achieved through the consensus-based process of the UNFCCC, The General Assembly could adopt our proposals by a simple majority vote, and therefore presents a genuine opportunity for significant progress. Like-minded vulnerable countries from Sagamata to the Pacific should prepare early, agree on a common strategy, and begin building the cross-regional support needed to secure concrete outcomes through the report process. We invite states to consider this and work with us through the Secretary-General's report process. From the mountains to the sea, the need is clear, the Court has clarified the law, But do we have the political will to take the next steps that justice requires? Thank you.

Thank you, Minister, for his very powerful remark. Now I would like to give the floor to Her Excellency Ms. Kanni Vignarajah, Assistant Secretary General and Regional Director of Asia and Pacific at the UNDP, another very important partner in Nepal to address global and climate change impact.

Thank you, moderator, honorable Ashish Kunal, excellencies. I'm going to cut to the chase and just agree with a lot of what has been said in the room. And I would like us to focus on maybe three choices, tough choices that your words have really put on the table. And these may sound technical. They are anything but. They are political choices, and they need to be negotiated. And I'm very glad I met a minister from Vanuatu in his home country recently, and his words are very, very strong. So three choices. First, a choice to let the new science and data guide our decisions. The real test is whether we can use this before disaster strikes, not after. It's quite amazing how the science is coming after, but we have all of this information and data of what's going on deep under the ground and also on the seas. So we can, with new satellite and AI mapping, show the breaking points well in advance. But this means a whole different approach to early warning systems and prevention. Second is a choice about design and build of infrastructure. Again, this is not a choice of engineering. These solutions are known. These are political choices, they're cross-border choices, and they're financial choices. But doing this right will save millions of people and millions in terms of cost. And a third is a choice about how we finance this future. The question is not whether we pay for adaptation, but how much we are willing to invest in prevention and resilience. So as a number of the ministers have said, concessional insurance and concessional financing that kicks in immediately is needed at a much greater scale than what we see today. But to enable this and really unpack this, it means the measure of the value and returns on investment has to change so that this investment then flows, as should insurance, in this direction. Now, UNDP, with all its partners here in the room, is working with Nepal and the other countries that spoke to really advocate for the new science, to turn the science into policy, the policy into investment, and the investment into more secure futures. To me, the term Sagar is really an interesting one because from one end, you can look at it as the mountains or the seas, but it's also curious that it's a choice of name for people. And it goes from Anglo-Saxon cultures to Sanskrit and Asian cultures. And in some, it means warrior, and in some, it means boundless wisdom. Well, to carry these negotiations forward, we're going to need really wise, tough warriors. Thank you.
Thank you, Yes, for your remarks. And now I would like to invite His Excellency, Mr. Jeyanta Jayasuriya, Permanent Representative of Sri Lanka to the United Nations, for his remark.

Thank you, Ambassador Thapa. Honourable Minister, Excellencies, Sri Lanka thanks Nepal and the co-sponsors for convening this discussion, and also wish to extend our profound sorrow and condolences to both the people and governments of Nepal and China for the losses that were caused due to the recent environmental disaster. Changes in mountains and river systems can be felt far from downstream. while the loss of land ice contributes to the rising seas facing island countries such as Sri Lanka. Last November, Cyclone Dikta brought severe flooding and landslide across Sri Lanka. It claimed 688 lives and affected 1.7 million people. Our experience has reinforced the importance of early warning and of having the capacity to act on it. Information must reach people on time and institutions must be ready to respond. Recovery must address environmental concerns, restore livelihoods, strengthen adaptive capacity, and reduce vulnerability to future disasters. At the national level, Sri Lanka is strengthening its institutional and policy frameworks for adaptation and disaster resilience. Vulnerable developing countries require greater and more accessible access to climate finance, technical assistance, and technology. transfer to strengthen preparedness, respond effectively to disasters, and recover in a resilient and sustainable manner. Mountain, downstream, and island communities experience climate change differently, but their futures are increasingly connected. The experiences of countries represented in this forum demonstrate the importance of collective action in building climate resilience. Sri Lanka stands ready to strengthen cooperation from Sagar Matha to the sea. I thank you.
I thank the Permanent Representative of Sri Lanka to the United Nations. Now I give the floor to the Co-Chairs of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, Mr. George Boensting, Norway.

Thank you, Chair. And let me just say that I'm presently here in the role as co-chair of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, but I'm also a representative of the Norwegian government. So let me just offer first my condolences and deep sympathy with the victims of the flash flood disaster and the solidarity with Nepal and the people in Nepal in this situation, both from the board, but also from the Norwegian government. This morning, we had an event on the urgent case for scaling up loss and damage finance organized by the government of the Philippines and in cooperation with the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage. Minister, you were also present there, and thank you for your participation. The Fund for Loss and Damage was established exactly to respond to these type of impacts of climate change. And as many of you will know, the Fund has also received a request for support to Nepal. And while the Fund is still not fully operational and it's in a stage of a pilot phase, the Board is fully committed to it's this request and it's presently considering an appropriate response to the request. Now taking my culture hat off, let me also say that Norway has contributed 10 million Norwegian kroner in humanitarian assistance to Nepal following the devastating floods, flash floods, and the funding will help provide shelter, clean water, health service, and other emergency assistance to effective communities and over stands with the people in Nepal in this difficult time. I would also just like to make another comment and which has been alluded to by several here and that is that knowledge, research and disaster preparedness is crucial for how we respond to a changing climate while we also must not lose sight of the urgency in tackling the root cause, which is emissions of greenhouse gases. Thank you. Now, Norway has partnered with Nepal and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, ICIMOD, since 1993 to support climate resilience, sustainable development and clean energy in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region. Some of the key focus areas of this partnership are the support of the SDGs regional collaboration among the eight HKH member countries, disaster preparedness and climate research. And we're also very proud of supporting ISMOHD's fifth action plan, focused on climate resilient and sustainable mountain future. And I will just end by saying that while there is an urgent and great need for financial and other support to Nepal now in this, in the aftermath of the flash flood tragedy, and unfortunately we will face similar and other types of loss and damage increasingly in the future. I think we have the knowledge. I would also just emphasise that maybe the best tribute we can pay to those who lost their lives is to learn from this tragedy and work together to reduce future risks. We will be there as a partner in that effort. Thank you.

I thank the co-chairs of the FRLD and also deeply appreciate the Norway's continued support to Nepal for the climate change and sustainable development. Now I give the floor to the Dr. Syed Mumtaz Pervez Special Assistant to the Prime Minister of Environment, Forest and Climate Affairs of Bangladesh.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, at the outset, I wish to convey Bangladesh's deepest condolences for the tragic loss of lives in the recent disaster in Nepal and China. Bangladesh stands firmly with the government and people of Nepal and China and remains in solidarity with them as they recover from its aftermath. I thank the organizers for choosing a theme that is very close to Bangladesh. Our country is located within the very mountain river delta sea system that lies at the heart of today's discussion. For Bangladesh and other countries along this mountain to sea continuum, the geography brings both opportunities and shared challenges. These river systems sustain agriculture, fisheries, freshwater ecosystems, and millions of livelihoods. They also offer important scope for regional cooperation in clean energy, water management, scientific research, disaster management, and connectivity. While extreme rainfall and floods in the upstream affect water flow, food security, and livelihoods in the downstream, sea level rise and salinity poses growing pressure on our delta and coastal communities. Again, the recent tragedy in Nepal and China is a painful reminder of how quickly hazards can turn into wider human and development losses. At the national level, Bangladesh has been strengthening resilience through long-term adaptation planning together with multi-hazard early warning and anticipatory action. However, when countries are so closely linked by shared geography, rivers, and climate systems, national efforts alone are not enough. A priority for our region, therefore, should be to strengthen cooperation on weather monitoring, hydrological data sharing, early warning and early action. Better and timely information can help others prepare faster for disasters and reduce cascading risks. This also requires stronger international support for climate resilient infrastructure, adaptation, loss and damage, technology transfer and capacity building. Nature is trying to send us a message. The planet is trying to send us a message. And this message is very simple. Stop global warming, stop carbon emission, and build unity. The question is whether we understand the importance of collective action, partnership, and this collaboration, and the message the planet is trying to send us. The Decade of Action for CRISPRic Science gives us a useful framework for deeper scientific cooperation. Keeping 1.5 degrees centigrade within reach must remain central because every additional fraction of warming increases risk across this connected system. Bangladesh would welcome taking such initiative forward as a practical platform for sustained cooperation among mountain, downstream, and coastal countries. We hope today's discussion will help build stronger and lasting partnerships around shared science, preparedness and resilience. I thank you.
Thank you. Now I would like to invite Dr. Bill Harris, CEO and Managing Director, Climate Analytics.

Thank you. Thank you, Honourable Minister, for convening this meeting. I'll be brief. Many of the things I would have liked to see have been done very well. But the climate crisis now, as we know, is here and now, and it's being measured in lives lost, communities displaced, ecosystems destabilised, development gains erased, especially for countries such as Nepal and the least developed country group. This year alone, we've seen some really extreme events. We've seen thousands of fatalities in Europe, hundreds of millions exposed to extreme heat in Asia, and now we've seen the catastrophic rock ice collapse in August in Nepal. These events are all together of a kind long predicted by the scientific community and are set to become more frequent in the future. Before going on, I'd like to add my condolences and deep sympathy to the people of Nepal for this disaster. The incident that we've just seen in Nepal will have reverberations for years to the communities affected in Nepal, and it will take them many years to rebuild. It's of a kind that is clear, I think, in terms of showing the limits to adaptation and where loss and damage starts. Now, what about the science of this? The science actually is showing that these kind of events, cascading rock disasters in high mountain regions, are going to get more frequent and more common and worse in their consequences unless we can rapidly reduce emissions. So this leads us then to the question of where we stand now on climate change and the issue of 1.5 degrees overshoot, which the United Nations Environment Programme has talked to us about. Current policies and commitments globally are far from limiting warming to 1.5, we're headed towards 2.6 degrees of warming, which means that without urgent action, we're headed towards a permanent overshoot of 1.5 degrees. Now, this doesn't weaken the importance of the Paris Agreement's 1.5 degree limit, nor does it justify discussion about aiming for higher levels of warming. I think instead it calls for doubling down on action and for governments everywhere to step up and accelerate their work on the transition away from fossil fuels. Legally, morally, and in every other way, 1.5 degrees remains the only defensible legal and moral limit that we can talk about. Overshoot has three critical dimensions which link to Saguamatha. How high temperatures rise beyond 1.5 degrees, how long they remain above, 1.5 and how quickly they can decline below. This is why the objectives before us now are to take a sufficient action to limit the magnitude and duration of overshoot and return warming well below 1.5 degrees as rapidly as possible. Every 10th of a degree above every year beyond 1.5 degrees will create more and more problems. We know that countries can step up, we know the economics is there to take sufficient action. I wanted to also just take the opportunity now to appreciate Nepal's initiative on the Sagarmatha dialogue and its connection to the mountains and the sea, which others have talked eloquently about. But I think this all leads to at least four actions, which I know others have referred to, but just in a way to summarize. Firstly, we simply have to have a rapid phase out of fossil fuels while accelerating renewable energy, energy efficiency, and methane reduction. This is the only way to reduce the warming that's going on. Second, we need to strengthen mountain science through long-term observation networks, open data, regional cooperation, and adequately funded research. Third, and this is connected to the second, we need to build early warning systems that cover the full risk chains. As we've seen in Switzerland, if that's there, then we can prevent a lot of harm to people. And this is another big priority for countries like Nepal and indeed every mountain region. Finally, the international community has to deliver, and it's been just reinforcing this, accessible and predictable finance for adaptation, loss and damage quickly and efficiently. I think I can leave my comments there. I think what we've seen in Nepal is that limits to adaptation have clearly been exceeded. dramatically into a loss and damage situation. And I think the challenge before governments now is to move forward on reducing emissions and beginning the transition away from fossil fuels. Thank you.

Thank you, Dr. Hari, for your remarks. And now I think we are running the time. Minister is to leave very soon, I think that's why Thank you so much, all the ministers, excellencies, colleagues, for your active participations as well as your contributions. Now, I would like to hand over the floor to Mr. Amrit Bhaduri, Foreign Secretary, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Nepal, for his closing remarks.

Thank you, Ambassador. Honorable ministers, excellencies, distinguished delegates, As we conclude this high-level special meeting, I wish to express our sincere appreciation and gratitude to the President of the General Assembly, ministers, ambassadors, and senior UN officials, and all delegates for their valuable insights and a strong spirit of solidarity and partnership for climate action. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Allow me to conclude with four clear messages from today's discussions. First, climate finance must reach the most climate vulnerable countries and communities. We need sustainable and substantially scaled up, predictable and accessible finance, particularly grant-based resources for adaptation and resilience. Second, We must prioritize early warning and early action to reach people in time. Advanced capabilities, from satellite observation to digital early warning systems, must be made accessible to developing and climate-vulnerable countries. Third, climate risk must be integrated across development and disaster risk planning, guided by our collective commitments under the Paris Agreement, COP commitments, and ICJ advisory opinions. Fourth, we must build a stronger regional and international cooperation and deeper solidarity and enhanced climate diplomacy. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, today's program is the manifestation of our deepest desire towards building a strong solidarity for climate action. Once again, let me thank you for your active and constructive engagement. Thank you. Back to you, Ambassador.
